### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

## October 8, 2026

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

...

## August 31, 2026

1. 23:30 UTC

### Rollout sandboxes are now just sandboxes

What we called rollout sandboxes is now just sandboxes, in the docs, in the pricing table on the front page, on your usage page, and on your invoice. A rollout is one thing you can run in a sandbox. Plenty of you run agent tool calls, builds, and untrusted code in them instead, and the shorter name covers all of it.

Nothing else moved. Every call, parameter, and id is unchanged, the rates are the same, and the docs section keeps its address. Three labels read differently. The two pricing rows are now Sandboxes (active) and Sandboxes (parked), and the line on your usage page and your invoice is Sandboxes. If a script of yours matches on those strings, that is the one thing to update.

...

results.title: How to make a market: an interview with Rich Jaycobs | SF Compute
results.author: Ethan Anderson
highlights:
# How to make a market: an interview with Rich Jaycobs#

September 18, 2026

How to make a market: an interview with Rich Jaycobs

...

A corn farmer knows a bushel costs $0.80 to grow, but not whether it sells for $1 or $2 at harvest. A GPU farmer has the same problem: hardware is paid for now, its hours sell later. Today the going rate is $4 a GPU-hour; a year out it could be anywhere from $2 to $5. That range is the risk to hedge.

results.title: Standard Intelligence and Roboflow access larger GPU clusters through SF Compute’s resale market | SF Compute
highlights:
Standard Intelligence and Roboflow access larger GPU clusters through SF Compute’s resale market | SF Compute

# Standard Intelligence and Roboflow access larger GPU clusters through SF Compute’s resale market#

September 28, 2026

Standard Intelligence and Roboflow scale with SF Compute

Mason Wheeler

SF Compute helps companies afford larger GPU clusters by letting them resell GPU hours to other teams. Customers can reserve enough GPUs for their biggest workloads, keep the hours they need, and sell unused hours to help reduce the reservation cost.

Those resold hours become short-term reservations for other teams, giving them access to large clusters for individual jobs without a long-term commitment.

## Standard Intelligence#

Standard Intelligence builds frontier models that learn from video to carry out computer tasks. They resell GPU hours outside of peak usage periods, which allows them to purchase larger, interconnected clusters to serve their most demanding workloads.

...

## Roboflow#

Resale from customers like Standard Intelligence makes more GPU capacity available for teams that need shorter commitments.

Roboflow, a computer vision startup, buys short-term GPU reservations on SF Compute. Their teams can run larger jobs and reserve just the time each job needs.

...

## A new model for compute providers#

In a traditional anchor tenant model, one customer makes a long-term commitment to a cluster at a fixed price. The provider earns the agreed contract revenue, regardless of how much of that capacity the customer uses.

Traditional Anchor Tenant Model

Long-term contract One long-term commitment

With SF Compute, that same commitment can generate an additional source of revenue. When the anchor tenant resells GPU hours to other teams, the provider earns a share of the resale fees on top of the original contract revenue.

SF Compute lets providers offer long-term anchor contracts, short-term burst contracts, or both. Shorter reservations can command higher hourly rates while costing customers less overall. Both contract types let customers resell GPU hours, with providers earning a share of resale fees on top of contract revenue.

Powered by SF Compute

Anchor tenant + resale One long-term commitment with resale to other tenants

Short-term burst + resale Multiple tenants over time
